subject: Default capture & deletion triggers — Acme Logistics
messages:
From: Selena Park <selena@acmelogistics.com>
To: alex_martinez@redwood.com
Cc: Jules Moreno <jules@acmelogistics.com>
Date: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Quick Q about what you store by default

Hi Alex,

We’re finalizing our security questionnaire and need a short, precise explanation of Redwood’s default capture behavior for hosted API traffic. Specifically: 

- Do you persist our raw inputs/prompts by default, or only metadata?
- Are generated outputs (completions) retained by default, and if so for how long?
- If we use streaming, are intermediate tokens/fragments persisted or discarded until the final completion?
- Is the KV cache or model cache ever written to durable storage?
- What triggers an automatic purge (TTL), and what is the customer-initiated deletion flow?

We’d also like to know what evidence you provide to show a deletion completed (for GDPR auditors). A one-paragraph answer plus any references would be perfect.

Thanks — Selena
Selena Park
Head of Engineering, Acme Logistics
selena@acmelogistics.com

From: Alex Martinez <alex_martinez@redwood.com>
To: Selena Park <selena@acmelogistics.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.com, rishi_malhotra@redwood.com
Date: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:00:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q about what you store by default

Hi Selena — thanks for the clear questions. TL;DR up front, then specifics.

TL;DR: For Redwood Hosted: by default we persist request metadata (timestamps, route, model) and request content (prompts) and generated outputs for short-term operational use. The default host retention window is 45 days for both requests and outputs unless you configure a different policy or select private/dedicated deployment. Streaming fragments are transient and not committed as final outputs until the stream completes. KV cache is not written to customer-visible durable storage. Customers can request immediate purge via API/Support and we provide audit evidence.

More detail: 
- Default scope: hosted API keeps request payloads (prompts), model outputs (completions), and operational metadata by default. This allows debugging, quality monitoring, rate-limiting, and safety tooling.
- Retention TTL: default 45 days (hosted). After TTL expires items are scheduled for purge and removed from primary stores; tombstone records in the audit system remain for a limited time to support compliance workflows.
- Streaming: intermediate token buffers are kept in-memory on the serving node and are not durably stored. Only the finalized completion (or explicitly flushed segments) enters the persisted artifact store.
- KV cache / model caches: these are ephemeral runtime caches and are never exposed as durable customer records; they are cleared on node restart and not included in retention stores.
- Customer-initiated deletion: customers can call the Data Erase endpoint or open a support request; we coordinate purge across caches, object stores, and logging backends. For hosted accounts we perform a region-aware purge and return a deletion confirmation with an internal request id you can use to track evidence.
- Proof of deletion: we provide an audit package that includes purge job ids, storage-object manifests removed (or lifecycle transitions), and an entry in the compliance audit log with timestamps and operator/service account details. For formal audits we supply a signed deletion summary (per request) and can map to the HubSpot ticket.

Attachments: I’m attaching a short CSV that maps default items to retention classes (retention-matrix-quickref.csv). Kim (cc’d) is our security lead — I’ll let her add formal language you can include in your questionnaire.

If helpful, we can run a 20-minute call to walk through this with your auditors next week.

— Alex
Alex Martinez

Alex — thanks, that helps a lot. A couple of follow-ups from the security team: 

1) For EU customers who choose the EU hosted region, does the 45-day default apply the same way, and are the purge operations performed within the EU region (no cross-border copies retained)?
2) For GDPR purposes: is an intermediate streaming token ever considered "persisted" if an interruption occurs (e.g., network drop) while streaming to the client?
3) For deletion evidence, do you provide cryptographic proofs (hash manifests) or just job ids and human-readable manifests? Our auditors want to see immutable evidence where possible.

Also, what SLA do you provide for executing a customer-initiated purge (how long until we can say data is removed)?

Selena
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Selena Park <selena@acmelogistics.com>, alex_martinez@redwood.com
Cc: rishi_malhotra@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q about what you store by default

Hi Selena — Kimberly here (Security & Compliance). I’ll provide the formal text you can paste into your questionnaire and answer your three follow-ups directly.

Official language you may include:
"By default Redwood Hosted stores request inputs (prompts), model outputs (completions), and operational metadata for a configurable retention window. The default retention window for hosted customers is 45 days. Customers using Redwood Dedicated or Private may configure retention to meet their regulatory requirements; Private deployments can be configured with no retained customer inputs. Streaming fragments remain in-memory on serving infrastructure and are not durably persisted as distinct records unless explicitly flushed or saved by the customer. Enacted purge operations are region-aware and executed against all durable artifact stores; audit logs record purge activity and are provided to the customer as deletion evidence."

Answers to your follow-ups: 
1) EU region: yes — when you select the EU hosted region, durable stores and purge operations are executed within the EU region. We do not intentionally replicate primary artifacts to non-EU regions; temporary cross-region replication for operational backups is avoided for EU accounts unless requested/approved.

2) Streaming interruptions: intermediate tokens buffered only in-memory are not considered persisted artifacts. If a transient failure causes the server to write a partial artifact (this is rare and logged as an exceptional event), we treat it as a persisted record and it follows the standard TTL/purge process; we provide incident detail to customers for such events.

3) Deletion evidence: our standard package includes purge job ids, storage-object manifests, and an audit log entry signed with internal service credentials. For customers requiring additional immutability we can provide hash manifests (SHA-256 checksums of stored objects) and an HSM-signed statement that the listed objects were removed as part of the purge. This is available on request for enterprise customers.

SLA for customer-initiated purge: standard hosted purge completes within 72 hours end-to-end for most accounts; for large-volume accounts or complex retention exceptions it can take up to 7 days. Dedicated/Private customers may have bespoke SLAs in contract.

Attachments included for your review: SOC2-evidence-guide.pdf (high-level evidence types we produce) and deletion-runbook.md (internal steps we execute for a purge). Reach out if you need this reworded for legal.
